## Abstract

Guidelines for primary prevention of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) recommend a risk calculator (ASCVD risk score) to estimate 10-year risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). As the necessary inputs are often missing, complementary approaches for opportunistic risk assessment are desirable.

To develop and test a deep-learning model (CXR CVD-Risk) that estimates 10-year risk of MACE from a routine chest radiograph (CXR) and compare its performance to the traditional ASCVD risk score for implications for statin eligibility.

Risk prediction study.

Outpatients potentially eligible for primary cardiovascular prevention.

CXR CVD-Risk was developed using cancer screening trial data. CXR CVD-Risk was externally validated in 1) 8,869 outpatients with unknown ASCVD risk because of missing inputs to calculate the ASCVD risk score and 2) 2,132 outpatients with known ASCVD risk where the ASCVD risk score could be calculated.

10-year MACE predicted by CXR CVD-Risk vs. the ASCVD risk score.

Among 8,869 outpatients with unknown ASCVD risk, those with CXR CVD-Risk ≥7.5% had higher risk of 10-year MACE after adjustment for risk factors (aHR 1.73 [1.47-2.03]). In the additional 2,132 outpatients with known ASCVD risk, CXR CVD-Risk predicted MACE beyond the traditional ASCVD risk score (aHR: 1.88 [1.24-2.85]).

Retrospective study design using electronic medical records.

Based on a single CXR, CXR CVD-Risk predicts 10-year MACE beyond the clinical standard and may help identify high-risk individuals with missing data to calculate the ASCVD risk score.

## INTRODUCTION

Cardiovascular diseases remain the most common cause of death (1–3). The American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association guidelines on the primary prevention of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) recommend a risk calculator for non-diabetic 40-75 year-olds with low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) between 70-190 mg/dl to estimating the risk of 10-year ASCVD as a guide to pharmacologic (e.g. statin) and other primary prevention (4). Risk is calculated using the ASCVD risk score, a multivariable regression model that takes 9 variables as inputs (5). While elevated 10-year ASCVD risk (≥7.5%) should prompt a risk discussion about initiating statin therapy, shared decision-making permits individualized approaches (6). However, as the necessary input variables to calculate the ASCVD risk score are often not available in the electronic medical record (EMR), other approaches for population-based screening are desirable to identify high-risk individuals likely to benefit from a statin. Opportunistic and automated risk assessment using data commonly available in the EMR (e.g. chest radiographs) could complement the ASCVD risk score and may be helpful to improve statin uptake.

Deep learning offers new possibilities for risk prognostication beyond currently established methods by using routine imaging such as chest radiographs ( CXR), which are among the most common tests in medicine (7–9). We previously demonstrated that deep learning can predict the risk of 12-year mortality, lung cancer, and biological age from CXR images independent of traditional risk factors in two randomized controlled trials (10–12). In addition, Kamel et al. reported that deep learning can estimate coronary artery calcium from CXRs (13).

Motivated by these results, our study explores whether deep learning can predict an individual’s risk of future major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) based on existing routine CXR images. Our hypothesis is that the CXR image contains information about future cardiovascular risk, that is complementary to established cardiovascular risk factors (e.g. blood pressure), when these data are not available in the EMR. To test this hypothesis, we first developed a deep-learning model that estimates the risk of cardiovascular mortality from a routine CXR image in a multicenter cancer screening trial. We then applied the model to predict future MACE in a separate outpatient population eligible for primary cardiovascular prevention, and compared the mode’s performance to the ASCVD risk score. The intent was to identify individuals who may potentially benefit from a statin, but who would not be recognized based on traditional metrics and available EMR data.

## METHODS

### Model development cohort

CXR CVD-Risk was developed in the Prostate, Lung, Colorectal, Ovarian (PLCO) Cancer Screening Trial (14,15). PLCO randomized 55-74 year-olds to lung cancer screening via chest radiography vs. usual care at 10 US sites from 1993-2001. Exclusion criteria were a history of prostate, lung, colorectal, or ovarian cancer or current treatment for any cancer (excluding basal and squamous cell skin cancer). In the chest radiograph arm, individuals received a baseline radiograph at enrollment (T0) and up to 3 annual follow-up radiographs (T1-T3) if no cancer was diagnosed. For the current study, a random subset of 80% (n=40,718) of participants was used for model development including chest radiographs from all four timepoints (T0-T3; n=147,801) (Supplementary Figure 1). The remaining 20% were used for internal testing (for results refer to Supplemental Methods). The only input to the model is a CXR image and the output is a probability of cardiovascular mortality between 0 and 1. Cardiovascular mortality was chosen as the output in PLCO, as information about non-fatal cardiovascular events was not available. Mortality was determined based on the National Death Index, communication with next of kin, and annual questionnaires(14,15). Cause of death was coded using International Classification of Disease (ICD) 9 codes (Supplementary Table 1). For further details on model development see Supplementary Methods. This study followed the Transparent Reporting of a Multivariable Prediction Model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis (TRIPOD) reporting guideline.

### Model testing cohorts

CXR CVD-Risk was externally validated without any retraining in a separate cohort of outpatients who had a CXR image taken between 2010-2011 (to ensure 10-year follow-up) at two hospitals (Massachusetts General Hospital and Brigham and Women’s Hospital) from the Mass General Brigham (MGB) healthcare system. These MGB hospitals did not participate in the PLCO trial, and the CXRs were obtained one to two decades after the end of PLCO’s enrollment, and so this can be considered as an external validation of the CXR CVD-Risk model. All presented results are based on actual observed 10-year incident MACE and are reported for the MGB testing dataset only, which was not used during any part of the model development process. All clinical information was retrieved from the MGB EMR (16). We tested CXR CVD-Risk performance in outpatient cohorts aged 50-75 years who 1) had an existing posterior-anterior CXR obtained through routine clinical care, 2) were not on a statin, 3) had no prevalent diabetes or LDL-C ≤70->190 mg/dl, if available, and 4) no prior history of MACE, coronary artery or peripheral artery disease with the aim to investigate the prognostic value in these individuals potentially eligible for primary ASCVD prevention. (Supplementary Figure 1).

Two cohorts were assessed, which represent two different clinical scenarios: first, when one or more of the inputs (e.g. LDL-C) necessary to calculate the ASCVD risk score was not available in the EMR, hereafter referred to as patients with unknown ASCVD risk. In this cohort, the intent was to identify individuals at increased risk of MACE who might be eligible for a statin and benefit from further workup but would otherwise be missed. Second, when all inputs to calculate the ASCVD Risk score were available within 2 years of the index CXR, hereafter referred to as patients with known ASCVD risk (Supplementary Figure 1). In this cohort, the aim was to compare the prognostic performance of the proposed CXR CVD-Risk score to the traditional ASCVD risk score. When a patient had multiple chest radiographs, the first radiograph was chosen. Prior atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease was defined using ICD codes for coronary artery disease, peripheral artery disease, and cerebral atherosclerosis (Supplementary Table 1)(17). Datasets were analyzed as complete case analysis and no data imputation was used.

Secondary use of PLCO data was approved by the National Cancer Institute, Bethesda, Maryland. The MGB Institutional Review Board, Boston, Massachusetts approved this retrospective study with waiver of informed consent.

### ASCVD risk score and statin eligibility

In the cohort where the traditional ASCVD risk score could be calculated, it was calculated using the standard inputs: age in years, sex, self-reported race (white and others vs. African American), smoking status, systolic blood pressure, hypertension treatment, total cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol and prevalent diabetes mellitus (5). Continuous risk scores were grouped into categories using standard thresholds (Low: <5%, Borderline: ≥5%-<7.5%, Intermediate: ≥7.5%-<20%, High: ≥20%)(18). As per 2019 ACC/AHA guidelines, statin eligibility was defined as a 10-year ASCVD risk ≥7.5% for non-diabetic 40-75 year-olds with LDL-C between 70-190 mg/dl.

### Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events

The primary outcome in the independent validation cohorts was incident MACE within 10 years of the CXR. MACE (fatal and non-fatal) was defined using published ICD-9 and -10 codes for acute stroke and myocardial infarction (17) (Supplementary Table 1). In the group of patients with known ASCVD risk, MACE events were manually confirmed using discharge summaries, cardiology reports and radiology reports. Date of last follow-up was defined as the last available data entry (radiology test, diagnosis code, or laboratory value) in the EMR. 232 (11%) individuals were censored as available follow-up was below 10 years.

### Statistical Analysis

Descriptive statistics are provided as mean±standard deviation or median and interquartile ranges (IQR) for continuous measures or frequencies and percentages for categorical measures.

To estimate the net benefit of CXR CVD-Risk vs. the ASCVD risk score across multiple thresholds, decision curves were calculated, which is a commonly used metric to estimate the benefit of true positives vs. the harm of false positives across a range of reasonable risk thresholds (19,20).

To measure discrimination of the CXR CVD-Risk vs. ASCVD risk estimates, we calculated and compared Harrel’s c-statistic (21) for 10-year incident MACE. In addition, calibration of CXR CVD-Risk vs. ASCVD risk score was assessed via calibration graphs and the Integrated Calibration Index (ICI)(22), which is a measure of differences between observed and predicted rates for 10-year MACE. Both discrimination and calibration are reported for the cohorts with unknown and known ASCVD risk separately.

Next, the continuous risk estimates of CXR CVD-Risk and the ASCVD risk score were stratified into groups based on established thresholds (Low: <5%, Borderline: ≥5%-<7.5%, Intermediate ≥7.5%-< 20%, High: ≥20%) and were assessed using reclassification tables.

For binary outcomes, survival analysis with Cox proportional hazards regression and cumulative incidence curves was used to assess the association between predicted risk categories and time to 10-year incident MACE for CXR CVD-Risk and ASCVD risk (survival R package version 3.2). The proportional hazards assumption was verified using scaled Schoenfeld residuals. Survival analysis was also used to assess the association between statin eligibility (10-year MACE risk ≥7.5%) and time to 10-year incident MACE. All statistical analyses were performed in R (version 4.0.2).

## RESULTS

### Demographics

Results are presented for two groups not on a statin but potentially eligible for primary prevention: 8,869 outpatients with unknown ASCVD risk because of missing data to calculate the traditional ASCVD risk score and 2,132 outpatients with known ASCVD risk as all input variables to calculate the ASCVD risk score were available.

#### Patients with unknown ASCVD risk:

Among the 8,869 outpatients with unknown ASCVD risk, 81.7% were Caucasian, 45.2% male and mean age was 60.3±6.7 years. Detailed patient demographics are provided in Supplementary Table 2. An overview of the study design is presented in Figure 1.

#### Patients with known ASCVD risk:

Among the 2,132 outpatients with known ASCVD risk where all inputs to calculate the ASCVD risk score were available, 75.5% were Caucasian, 35.5% were male and the mean age was 59.5±6.6 years (Supplementary Table 2). This comprised only 19.4% (2,132/11,001) of all individuals meeting the inclusion criteria (aged 50-75 years, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol 70-190 mg/dl, if available, no prevalent diabetes and no prior MACE).

### Distribution of CXR CVD-Risk vs. the traditional ASCVD risk score and reclassification of 10-year MACE

Distributions of the CXR CVD-Risk and traditional ASCVD risk score estimates by established risk categories for the 2,132 patients with known ASCVD risk are presented in Supplementary Table 3.

A confusion matrix of CXR CVD-Risk vs. traditional ASCVD risk categories for 10-year MACE is presented in Table 1, indicating a largely similar risk estimation per risk categories for CXR CVD-Risk and the traditional ASCVD risk score.

Moreover, CXR CVD-Risk also stratified among Low, Borderline and Intermediate ASCVD risk score groups (risk of 10-year MACE for Low: 1.3%-4.2%; Borderline: 2.5%-6.3%; Intermediate: 4.3%-13.3%) whereas this effect was not seen for the High ASCVD risk groups (Table 1).

In addition, the CXR CVD-risk model also revealed a clear risk stratification among the 8,869 patients with unknown ASCVD risk but potentially eligible for primary cardiovascular prevention (Table 1).

### Statin eligibility

With statin eligibility defined as ASCVD risk ≥7.5%, the CXR CVD-Risk and traditional ASCVD risk score estimates were concordant for statin eligibility in 69.7% of patients (1485/2132, Table 2). In the 30.3% (647/2,132) discordant cases, the CXR CVD-Risk estimates upclassified 50.4% (326/647) of patients as statin eligible (MACE rate 4.6% [15/326]).

In the cohort where the ASCVD risk score could not be calculated due to missing inputs in the EMR, a CXR-CVD Risk ≥7.5% identified a group with a high 10-year observed incidence of MACE (11.8% [500/4245]) who may benefit from primary cardiovascular prevention (Table 2).

Risk reclassification tables for individuals who did and did not go on to MACE, based on a CXR CVD-Risk or ASCVD risk score ≥7.5% are provided in Supplementary Table 4.

### Decision curves

In the cohort of 8,869 outpatients with unknown ASCVD risk, CXR CVD-Risk had a higher net benefit than baseline strategies of treating everyone and treating no one (Figure 2a) across risk thresholds close to the 7.5% standard for statin eligibility. In the cohort of 2,132 outpatients with known ASCVD risk, the traditional ASCVD risk score showed a small but higher net benefit compared to the CXR CVD-Risk model (Figure 2b). The highest benefit was observed for both CXR CVD-Risk and the ASCVD Risk score for lower risk thresholds <7%.

### 10-year observed incident MACE

#### Patients with unknown ASCVD risk:

The 10-year incident MACE rate in the 8,869 patients with unknown ASCVD risk was 8.9% (785/8,869) over a median follow-up of 10.3 (IQR: 7.2-10.7) years. Those who experienced MACE were older (61.8 vs. 60.1 years) and more likely male (58.5% vs. 43.9%) than those without MACE (Supplementary Table 2). Cumulative incidence curves showed a graded association between CXR CVD-Risk categories and 10-year incident MACE (Figure 3). Based on the observation of a number of early incident MACE events, a cumulative incidence curve excluding all patients who experienced MACE within six months after the CXR is also provided (Supplementary Figure 2).

Among all 8,869 outpatients with unknown ASCVD risk, 47.9% (4,245/8,869) were statin eligible according to the CXR CVD-Risk estimates (CXR CVD-Risk ≥7.5% estimated 10-year risk of MACE). Of those classified as statin eligible by CXR CVD-Risk, 11.8% (500/4,245) developed incident MACE compared to 6.2% (285/4,624) of those classified as ineligible. In univariable Cox proportional hazard regression, the univariate hazard ratio for 10-year incident MACE was 2.19 (95% CI 1.90-2.54) for eligible vs. non-eligible patients (Supplementary Table 5). This association remained robust after adjustment for available clinical risk factors (age, sex, race, current smoking, prevalent hypertension): adjusted HR 1.73 (95% CI 1.47-2.03).

Further information on discrimination and calibration are provided in Supplementary Results.

#### Patients with known ASCVD risk:

The incident MACE rate in the 2,132 patients with known ASCVD risk was 4.8% (102/2,132) over a median follow-up of 10.4 (IQR: 10.1-10.8) years. Those who experienced MACE were older (62.1 vs. 59.4 years), more likely male (49.0% vs. 34.8%) and current smokers (23.5% vs. 11.4%) than those without MACE (Supplementary Table 2).

The mean estimates for 10-year MACE risk were 8.6% (SD 6.9) for CXR CVD-Risk and 7.2% (SD 6.0) for the traditional ASCVD risk score. The individuals who suffered an incident MACE had a higher estimated risk score than those who did not for both CXR CVD-Risk and the ASCVD risk score estimates (Supplementary Table 2). Distributions of the CXR CVD-Risk and traditional ASCVD risk score estimates by established risk categories are presented in Supplementary Table 3. The association between CXR CVD-Risk as well as the traditional ASCVD risk score and time to incident MACE was estimated using cumulative incidence curves by the four ordinal risk categories (Figure 3), which show a strong separation for both the CXR CVD-Risk and the traditional ASCVD risk score. Further information on discrimination and calibration are provided in Supplementary Results.

Among the 2,132 patients with known ASCVD risk, CXR CVR-Risk identified 37.0% (787/2,132) as statin-eligible while the traditional ASCVD risk score identified 36.8% (782/2,132). Of those identified as statin eligible by CXR CVD-Risk, 7.6% (60/787) developed incident MACE vs. 3.1% (42/1,345) of those identified as ineligible (HR 2.77 [95% CI 1.87-4.11]). In contrast, among those identified as eligible for statin treatment by the traditional ASCVD risk score, 8.7% (68/782) developed incident MACE compared to 2.5% (34/1,350) among those identified as ineligible (HR 3.88 [95% CI 2.57-5.85]). (Supplementary Table 5).

To test whether CXR CVD-Risk predicts 10-year incident MACE beyond the traditional ASCVD risk score, the hazard radio for statin eligibility by CXR CVD-Risk adjusted for the traditional ASCVD risk score was calculated. In this model, the hazard of 10-year incident MACE was 88% higher for statin eligible (aHR: 1.88 [95% CI 1.24-2.85]) vs. ineligible patients independent of the traditional ASCVD risk score.

## DISCUSSION

This study introduces a deep learning model (CXR CVD-Risk) that identifies individuals at high 10-year risk of MACE, based on a single chest radiograph image. Opportunistic screening of existing chest radiographs could complement the traditional ASCVD risk score to identify patients at high cardiovascular risk who may benefit from primary prevention, and would be of particular impact in the majority (81%, 8,869/11,001) of our cohort where the inputs to calculate the 10-year ASCVD risk score were not available in the EMR.

Our major results are that 1) only 19% (2,132/11,001) of patients potentially eligible for primary cardiovascular prevention had all necessary inputs available to calculate the traditional guideline recommended ASCVD risk score to estimate 10-year MACE risk, 2) in these patients with known ASCVD risk, CXR CVD-Risk had similar performance and additive value to the traditional ASCVD risk score and 3) in the remaining 81% (8,869) of patients who are potentially eligible for primary cardiovascular prevention but with unknown ASCVD risk due to missing inputs to calculate the traditional ASCVD risk score, those identified as statin eligible by CXR CVD-Risk had a 1.5 fold increased risk of 10-year incident MACE compared to those classified as ineligible independent of available baseline cardiovascular risk factors. These findings suggest that CXR CVD-Risk could enable population-based opportunistic screening using routine chest radiographs to identify high-risk individuals who would benefit from primary ASCVD prevention with statins but are currently unrecognized.

Chest radiographs are the most commonly performed imaging test(9) and are acquired during the course of many patients’ clinical workup at low cost(23) and radiation dose(24). Although most chest radiographs obtained in daily routine are negative in that no intervention is necessary, the results of this and previously published studies(10–12) suggest that deep learning can capture imaging features beyond traditional findings (e.g. enlarged heart silhouette, lung nodules) with valuable prognostic and potentially actionable information. In this context, we consider the proposed model as a new risk score/factor that, instead of traditional risk factors (e.g. diabetes or smoking), takes a CXR as input to estimate the underlying risk of an individual, which could be used as additional input variable for larger models in the future. However, we do not recommend ordering a chest radiograph specifically to estimate ASCVD risk as a population wide screening examination. Instead, a more pragmatic approach could be to implement the CXR CVD-Risk model as an automatic tool into the electronic medical record to opportunistically analyze existing and readily available routine chest radiographs, which for example, were available for 20% of those aged 40-79 years who had an outpatient visit in January or February 2022 at our institution. This could be done cost-effectively and with minimal disruption of current clinical workflows with the potential to substitute for traditional ASCVD risk assessment if the necessary information is not available. Whenever an individual with increased risk of 10-year MACE is identified, an automatic flag could be raised to notify the treating physician to perform further in-depth and personalized risk evaluation and to initiate preventive measures. This study will serve as the foundation for future prospective trials to assess whether implementation can improve decision making and patient outcomes.

These results are limited by the retrospective study design across two hospitals using risk factors and outcomes extracted from the electronic medical record. Our cohort included patients who had a routine chest radiograph, lipid panel, and blood pressure measurements within a 2-year period, and thus are likely at higher risk compared to the general population. ICD-based phenotyping may have low specificity for outcome determination; we manually validated events in the 2,132 patients with inputs available to calculate ASCVD risk but may be overestimating the event rate in the broader cohort. Guidelines for primary prevention apply to individuals 40-75 years of age; however, we only included individuals 50-75 years of age, as the CXR CVD-Risk model was developed in people 55-74 years of age. Moreover, as our study cohort primarily consisted of non-Hispanic whites, further studies are necessary to assess generalizability in racially and ethnically diverse cohorts and in other care settings. Finally, convolutional neural networks are inherently “black boxes,” and CXR CVD-Risk estimates are difficult to explain on an individual basis as they quantify the underlying 10-year risk rather than a specific disease or imaging feature that directly leads to MACE. This is a common limitation of CNNs that may limit their application to clinical decision making and is an active area of research(25).

In conclusion, based on a single routine chest radiograph image, a deep learning model can predict 10-year incident MACE. The model could be applied in the majority of patients where lipids or other inputs to the ASCVD risk score are not available. Opportunistic screening of chest radiographs may help identify individuals at high risk of cardiovascular disease, prompting risk factor assessment and targeted prevention.
